summary: Explains the IP Router Alert Option, which flags a packet so that routers along the path look at it more closely. It discusses the security risks of the option and gives guidelines for protocols that use it, such as RSVP and IGMP. It is a best current practice and updates RFC 2113 and RFC 2711.

plainLanguage.summary: The Router Alert is a flag in an IP packet that asks routers along the way to give it extra attention. That is useful for some signalling protocols, but it also lets anyone slow a router down. This RFC says where it is safe to use and how to live with it.

questions: what is the ip router alert option
is router alert a security risk
how do routers handle router alert packets
should router alert be used across the internet
subtitle: Why the Router Alert option is risky on the open Internet, and where it is safe.

tldr.problem: The IP Router Alert option asks every router on the path to look at a packet more closely, and a router cannot reliably tell the packets it cares about from the ones an attacker sent.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reviews the security exposure of the option in IPv4 and IPv6, then divides deployment into cases: the open Internet, where the option should not be relied on end to end, and controlled environments, where it can be used safely.
tldr.outcome: Service providers are told to protect their networks strongly against Router Alert based attacks, and router implementations are given guidance on filtering, rate limiting, tunnelling and forwarding behaviour that reduces the exposure.

today: RFC 6398 is a Best Current Practice, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 2113 and RFC 2711, which define the IPv4 and IPv6 Router Alert Options.

sections.title: What the Router Alert Option Does
sections.content:
RFC 2113 and RFC 2711 define the IPv4 and IPv6 Router Alert Options, and this document refers to both collectively as the IP Router Alert. The option alerts transit routers to more closely examine the contents of an IP packet.

Several protocols make use of it: the Resource reSerVation Protocol (RSVP), Pragmatic General Multicast (PGM), the Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP), Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD), Multicast Router Discovery (MRD), and Next Steps in Signaling General Internet Signaling Transport (GIST).

The document describes the security concerns of the option, gives guidelines for its use, recommends that it not be used for end-to-end applications over the Internet, presents controlled environments where it can be deployed effectively and safely, offers recommendations on protection approaches for service providers, and finishes with generic recommendations for router implementations. Possible future enhancements to the option, aimed at reducing the security risks, are outside the scope of the document; one such proposal is discussed in a separate Internet-Draft, but no extension had been adopted by the IETF at the time of writing.

The IPv6 base specification defines the hop-by-hop options extension header, used to carry optional information that must be examined by every node along a packet's delivery path, and the IPv6 Router Alert Option is one such hop-by-hop option. Similar security concerns apply more generally to the concept of that extension header, but addressing the broader concept would need additional material, such as whether the effectiveness of an attack depends on how many options are included, so it is kept out of scope. The IPv4 base specification defines a general notion of IPv4 options, and the IPv4 Router Alert Option is one of them. Similar concerns apply to IPv4 options in general, but other IPv4 options are often blocked in firewalls and are not widely used, so the practical risks they present are largely nonexistent.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is a request for extra attention along the path. It is used by signalling and multicast protocols, and this RFC is about the trouble it causes.

sections.title: Fast Path and Slow Path
sections.content:
The document uses three loosely defined terms. The fast path is the hardware or application-specific integrated circuit processing path for packets, the nominal processing path within a router for IP datagrams. The slow path is the software processing path, a sub-nominal path for packets that require special processing or differ from the assumptions made in fast-path heuristics. The next level protocol is the protocol carried inside the IP datagram, identified in IPv4 by the IANA protocol number in the 8-bit Protocol field of the header and in IPv6 by the IANA protocol number in the 8-bit Next Header field.

These terms matter because the whole problem is about where a router decides to handle a Router Alert packet. A packet handled in software competes with everything else the router does in software, and a packet handled in hardware does not.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers have a fast lane for ordinary traffic and a slow lane for anything unusual. A Router Alert packet usually ends up in the slow lane, which is where the danger lies.

sections.title: Why the Router Alert Is a Risk
sections.content:
The option is defined as a mechanism that alerts transit routers to more closely examine packet contents, and the security risks are already known: flooding a router with bogus or simply undesired datagrams containing the option could affect its operation in undesirable ways. If the router punts such datagrams to the slow path, the attack could consume a significant share of the slow path and lead to packet drops there, affecting all other applications and protocols operating in that path, and so resulting in a denial of service.

RFC 2113 specifies no mechanism for identifying different users of the option, and RFC 2711 specifies a very limited one, so many fast-switching implementations punt most or all marked packets into the slow path unless configured to ignore or drop them systematically. Some deployed routers can and do process these packets inside the fast path.

Some implementations use the next level protocol as a discriminator for the punting decision, but that only allows coarse triage, for two reasons. The next level protocol is the same when the option is used for different applications of the same protocol, such as RSVP against RSVP-TE, or for different contexts of the same application, such as different levels of RSVP aggregation. And some protocols that require punting are carried over a transport protocol, because they need the services of that transport, because the protocol does not justify allocating a scarce next level protocol value, or because not relying on a widely deployed transport protocol is likely to cause deployment problems with common middlebox behaviour such as firewalls or NATs discarding packets of unknown protocols.

Some implementations can also take the Value field inside the option into account, but only one value, zero, was defined in RFC 2113, and no IANA registry for IPv4 Router Alert values was available until RFC 5350, so most implementations could not classify usefully on that basis in the fast path. Some implementations are reported to ignore the Value field completely and process any packet carrying an IPv4 Router Alert regardless of its value.

RFC 2711 mentions that limiting the use of the option by rate or other means is a way of protecting against a potential attack. But if the granularity of the rate limiting is not fine enough to distinguish the packets of interest from the unwanted ones, an attack could still severely degrade the protocols that do depend on the option.

In a nutshell, the option does not provide a convenient universal mechanism to distinguish reliably between the packets of interest and the unwanted ones, and short of router-specific mechanisms the slow path is at risk of being flooded.
sections.plainLanguage: A router has no reliable way to tell a genuine signalling packet from one an attacker made up, so it has to treat them all the same, and that is what makes the flood possible.

sections.title: The Recommendation for the Open Internet
sections.content:
Because of the security concerns, network operators SHOULD actively protect themselves against externally generated IP Router Alert packets. Because there are no convenient universal mechanisms to triage between desired and undesired packets, operators often protect themselves in ways that isolate them from externally generated ones, either by tunnelling the packets so that the option is hidden across the network, or by mechanisms that result in occasional, for example rate-limited, or systematic drops of such packets.

Applications and protocols SHOULD NOT be deployed with a dependency on processing of the Router Alert Option, as currently specified, across independent administrative domains in the Internet. The document calls this the Peer Model, because core routers in different administrative domains would take part in processing Router Alert datagrams associated with the same signalling flow.

While the recommendation is framed in terms of Router Alert, the fundamental risk operators want to preclude is allowing devices and protocols outside their administrative domain, and therefore not controlled, to tap into the control plane of their core routers. Similar concerns would result whether that access came through the Router Alert Option or through any other mechanism such as deep packet inspection. The concern is with end-to-end signalling in a Peer Model across domains, so operators would typically not want their core routers to take part in end-to-end signalling with external uncontrolled devices through the open Internet, and therefore prevent such deployment through their network, whether or not the signalling uses Router Alert.
sections.plainLanguage: On the open Internet, a signal that every core router has to act on is an invitation to trouble, so protocols should not depend on it across administrative borders.

sections.title: Where the Router Alert Is Safe to Use
sections.content:
In some controlled environments, such as within a single administrative domain, the administrator can determine that Router Alert packets will only be received from trusted and well-behaved devices, or can establish that specific protection mechanisms such as filtering and rate limiting are sufficient against the plausible attacks. In that case an application relying on these packets, such as RSVP, can be deployed safely. A private enterprise network firewalled from the Internet and using RSVP reservations for voice and video flows is an example.

Several administrative domains may also have a special relationship, cooperating so tightly that they effectively operate as a single trust domain, where one domain is willing to trust another with respect to traffic injected across the boundary, that is, the downstream domain trusts that traffic injected at the boundary has been validated and filtered by the upstream domain. Where that trust has been established for Router Alert packets, the application can be deployed safely. The team operating multimedia endpoints and the team operating the network inside one company might be an example.

In other environments the administrator can reliably ensure that Router Alert packets from any untrusted device are prevented from entering a trusted area, for instance by having the routers straddling the trust boundary always encapsulate those packets, without setting the Router Alert or an equivalent option in the encapsulating header, as they pass through the trusted area. The risks are then removed or greatly reduced in the trusted area, even if the option is used inside it, for example for RSVP-TE. A service provider running RSVP-TE within its own network is an example of such a protected environment.

The Overlay Model adds a further case. Where the sites of a network are interconnected through a service provider network that protects itself from Router Alert messages without dropping them as they transit, an application relying on these packets in the sites, but not inside the provider network, can be safely deployed. The document calls this a Water-Tight Overlay: the option is used in the customer network on top of, and completely transparently to, the provider network, and packets from the customer network cannot leak inside the provider network. A private enterprise intranet realized as a VPN over a provider network might be an example.

A Leak-Controlled Overlay covers the case where the provider processes Router Alert packets on its edge routers and protects those edge routers with filtering and rate limiting, while protecting its core routers without dropping the messages as they transit. An application can then be deployed in the customer sites and on the provider's edges, but not in the provider's core. The option is used in the customer network transparently over the provider's core, and packets from the customer network leak inside the provider's edges but not inside its core.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside a network you control, or inside a tunnel that hides the option from everyone else, the risk is manageable. The document names four situations where it is.

sections.title: How a Service Provider Protects Its Network
sections.content:
Since the option opens a denial-of-service vector into the router control plane, a service provider MUST implement strong protection of its network against attacks based on it.

Because some applications benefit from the option in an Overlay Model, where the packets are exchanged transparently on top of a service provider, a provider protecting its network SHOULD use mechanisms that avoid, or at least minimize, the dropping of end-to-end Router Alert packets other than those involved in an attack.

Several examples are given. If the provider runs no protocol depending on the option, it might simply turn off the punting and processing of Router Alert packets on its routers, which ensures that end-to-end packets transit its network transparently and safely. Using selective filtering and rate limiting, a provider can protect a protocol that depends on the option within its network, such as RSVP-TE, while transporting packets carrying another protocol that might be used end to end. The provider might additionally use protocol-specific mechanisms that reduce the dependency on the option, and the use of RSVP refresh reduction mechanisms is given as an example, since that allows existing Path and Resv states to be refreshed without the option.

Using the tunnelling mechanisms of RFC 6178, a provider can safely protect a protocol that depends on the option within its network while transporting Router Alert packets carrying another protocol that might be used end to end. Tunnelling over an MPLS backbone is well understood, but tunnelling over a non-MPLS IP backbone presents issues, in particular for determining where to forward the encapsulated datagram, and is not common practice at the time of writing.

As a last resort, a provider with no means to transport end-to-end Router Alert packets safely can drop them, with the undesirable consequence of preventing the Overlay Model use of the option over that network and preventing its users from deploying a number of valid applications.
sections.plainLanguage: A provider has to defend its routers, but it should also try not to break other people's protocols, so the RFC lists ways to filter the flood without discarding the traffic entirely.

sections.title: Guidelines for Router Implementations
sections.content:
A router implementation of the option SHOULD include protection mechanisms against Router Alert based denial-of-service attacks, as appropriate for its deployment environment. That can include the ability of an edge router to tunnel received Router Alert packets when forwarding them over the core, and, though not always available from current implementations, new implementations MAY include selective, possibly dynamic, filtering and rate limiting of such packets.

Router implementations SHOULD offer the configuration option to simply ignore the presence of IP Router Alert in IPv4 and IPv6 packets. That permits the packets to transit a network segment without presenting an adverse operational security risk to that segment, provided the operator never uses the option for any purpose.

If an IP packet contains the option but the next level protocol is not explicitly identified as a protocol of interest by the router examining it, the behaviour is not explicitly defined by RFC 2113, but it is implied, and the definition of RSVP assumes that the packet will be forwarded using normal forwarding based on the destination IP address. A router implementation SHOULD therefore forward within the fast path, subject to all normal policies and forwarding rules, a packet carrying the option whose next level protocol is not of interest to that router. The not-punting behaviour protects the router from denial-of-service attacks using packets of a protocol unknown to it, and the forwarding behaviour contributes to transparent end-to-end transport of such packets.

Similarly, an implementation MAY support selective forwarding within the fast path, or punting, based on the Value field of the option, which would allow protection against denial-of-service attacks using packets with a value that is not relevant for that router, such as the nesting levels of aggregated RSVP reservations.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that does not care about the protocol in a marked packet should just forward it as ordinary traffic, rather than send it to its slow processing lane where an attacker can fill it up.

viz.caption: WHY A ROUTER CANNOT TELL GOOD PACKETS FROM BAD ONES

items.title: No user identification
items.text: The option says nothing about who sent the packet, so anyone can set it.

items.title: Coarse protocol check
items.text: The protocol number is the same for RSVP and RSVP-TE, and for different aggregation levels.

items.title: Transported over TCP or UDP
items.text: A protocol carried over a transport protocol hides which one it is.

items.title: One IPv4 value
items.text: Only the value zero was defined, so the value field gives little to work with.

items.title: Coarse rate limiting
items.text: A limit too broad to separate the wanted packets still lets the flood through.

cells: Nothing; the RFC recommends against it
Trust in the devices, or filtering and rate limiting
In the customer sites, over a provider network
The provider hides the option from its core
In the customer sites and on the provider's edges
The provider filters and rate limits at the edge only

viz.caption: WHAT ROUTER IMPLEMENTATIONS ARE ASKED TO DO

items.title: Offer a switch to ignore it
items.text: A configuration option that treats the option as absent.

items.title: Forward unfamiliar protocols
items.text: A marked packet whose protocol is of no interest stays in the fast path.

items.title: Use the value field
items.text: Forwarding or punting can depend on the value inside the option.

items.title: Filter and rate limit
items.text: Selective, possibly dynamic, filtering of marked packets.

items.title: Tunnel at the edge
items.text: Encapsulate marked packets when forwarding them over the core.
